summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application (sqli package: views, routes, DAOs, middlewares, services, auth/jinja utils, schema), templates, migrations, Docker/compose, and config. The app is deliberately vulnerable and the code confirms it: a classic SQL injection in Student.create, global disabling of Jinja2 autoescaping leading to stored XSS, unsalted MD5 password hashing, CSRF protection commented out, non-HttpOnly session cookies, and missing authorization on state-changing endpoints. Overall risk is critical: unauthenticated attackers can achieve SQL injection and stored XSS, and perform privileged actions. Static assets (materialize/jquery) were not audited line-by-line.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via unparameterized name interpolation
findings.description: The create() method builds the INSERT statement by Python %-formatting the attacker-controlled student name directly into the SQL string instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The name comes straight from the untrusted POST body in views.students (data['name']) with no validation (the STUDENT_SCHEMA trafaret is never applied here) and the /students/ POST endpoint has no authentication, so any anonymous user can inject arbitrary SQL. A payload like Robert'); DROP TABLE students;-- or a stacked/subquery payload can read or destroy data, extract the users table (including pwd_hash) via error/stacked queries. This is the primary, directly reachable vulnerability.
findings.evidence:
views.py:54-57 -> data = await request.post(); await Student.create(conn, data['name']).
student.py:42-43: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  then cur.execute(q) with no params. Contrast with the safe parameterized queries in course.py/review.py/mark.py which pass a params dict to execute().
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with Python string formatting on user input. Also apply STUDENT_SCHEMA validation in the view.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so every template variable is rendered as raw HTML unless an explicit |e filter is used. Multiple templates emit untrusted, persisted data without escaping: course.jinja2 renders review.review_text, course.title and course.description (line 14-22), and students.jinja2 renders the student name (line 16). Course reviews can be created by any unauthenticated user (POST /courses/{id}/review has no auth and no output encoding), so an attacker can store <script> payloads that execute in every visitor's and admin's browser. Because session cookies are not HttpOnly (see separate finding) this leads to full session hijacking.
findings.evidence:
app.py:33-35: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader(...), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False).
course.jinja2:22 {{ review.review_text }} (unescaped) fed by Review.create from views.review (views.py:119-129, no auth).
students.jinja2:16 {{ name }} unescaped.
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping: pass autoescape=jinja2.select_autoescape(['html','jinja2']) (or autoescape=True) to setup_jinja, and rely on explicit |safe only where output is known-trusted. Review templates to remove manual unescaped sinks.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (evaluate/students/courses)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns marks to students but has no authentication or authorization check, even though the UI only exposes it to admins (course.jinja2 gates the form behind auth_user.is_admin). Any anonymous user can POST to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} and insert arbitrary marks. The same missing-authorization flaw applies to the student-creation branch in views.students (views.py:54-57) and the course-creation branch in views.courses (views.py:86-90), which also perform writes with no auth check. Only logout uses the @authorize decorator.
findings.evidence: views.py:134-153 evaluate(): no @authorize decorator; directly calls Mark.create after only validating points. authorize()/get_auth_user exist in utils/auth.py but are applied only to logout (views.py:156). Compare course.jinja2:41 which hides the evaluate form behind {% if auth_user.is_admin %}, showing the intended restriction is not enforced server-side.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate (and appropriate @authorize() checks to the student/course/review creation paths), enforcing authorization on the server rather than relying on template-level hiding.

findings.title: Unsalted MD5 used for password hashing and verification
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash against a plain unsalted MD5 of the supplied password, and the fixtures store passwords as md5('...'). MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: stolen hashes (e.g. via the SQL injection above) are trivially cracked with rainbow tables/GPU brute force, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. The comparison is also non-constant-time.
findings.evidence: user.py:41 return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(). migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13 store md5('superadmin'), md5('password'), etc.
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt/scrypt/argon2) via passlib, and compare with a constant-time verify. Rehash existing passwords on next login.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
findings.description: A functioning CSRF middleware exists (middlewares.csrf_middleware) and templates render a _csrf_token hidden field, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no POST request's CSRF token is ever validated. Combined with session cookies sent on cross-site requests, an attacker can forge requests (create students/courses, submit reviews with XSS payloads, assign marks, log the victim out) from a victim's authenticated browser.
findings.evidence: app.py:24-30 middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]. middlewares.py:25-38 defines csrf_middleware that validates session['_csrf_token'] against form data on POST, but it is never registered.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure all state-changing forms submit the token (most already do via csrf_token()).

findings.title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: The Redis-backed session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Chained with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, an attacker's injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie and hijack authenticated/admin sessions. The cookie is also not marked Secure, so it can leak over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Create the storage with httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True when served over HTTPS.
